title: Estimates of temporary employment
text:
In this exercise, we will recreate ONS labour market analysis published online in the table EMP07 Temporary Employees. Currently, this table is updated four times a year in February, May, August and November using the Quarterly Labour Force Survey (QLFS).
Learning outcomes:

To become more familiar with QLFS datasets.
To become familiar with producing weighted population estimates
To understand how some ONS estimates are produced



The data used in this exercise relates to an estimate published by the ONS for October-December 2024.
To follow the exercise, you need to access the relevant dataset from the UK Data Service: Quarterly Labour Force Survey, October - December, 2024.



One you have downloaded the data, save it somewhere accessible, for example in a folder named LFS_exercises. We can now begin analysing the data using R. First let’s load the packages that are are going to need:

library(haven)
library(dplyr)
library(survey)
library(srvyr)


## #setwd ("~/LFS_exercises")


# Inport  the data from a Stata format dataset
lfs_od24 <- read_dta("lfsp_od24_eul_pwt24.dta")

Inspect the dataset and find out the number of cases and variables.

ncol(lfs_od24) # Number of columns

[1] 803

nrow(lfs_od24) # Number of rows (observations)

[1] 63069

dim(lfs_od24)  # Both

[1] 63069   803



QuestionsAnswers



How many variables are there?




803




As there are many variables in the dataset, let’s create a copy with just the variables we will use. We can also use this opportunity to make the variable categories easier to understand by converting them into factors. For greater clarity, we also remove unused categories of categorical variables using droplevels().

mydata <- lfs_od24 |> 
  select(PERSNO, PWT24, JBTP101, FTPT, INECAC05, JOBTYP, SEX)|>
  mutate(across(.cols=JBTP101:SEX, 
                .fns=as_factor,"both")
         )|>
  droplevels()




We can have a look at the raw data by using head() or View()

head(mydata)

# A tibble: 6 × 7
  PERSNO    PWT24     JBTP101             FTPT             INECAC05 JOBTYP SEX  
  <dbl+lbl> <dbl+lbl> <fct>               <fct>            <fct>    <fct>  <fct>
1 1         706       [-9] Does not apply [-9] Does not a… [31] In… [-9] … [2] …
2 2         887       [-9] Does not apply [1] Full time    [2] Sel… [-9] … [1] …
3 1         598       [-9] Does not apply [-9] Does not a… [31] In… [-9] … [2] …
4 1         879       [-9] Does not apply [-9] Does not a… [31] In… [-9] … [2] …
5 2           0       [-9] Does not apply [-9] Does not a… [31] In… [-9] … [1] …
6 1         793       [-9] Does not apply [2] Part time    [1] Emp… [1] P… [2] …

View(mydata) # A nicer looking output

Now let’s examine all variables in more detail.

mydata |> select(JBTP101, FTPT, INECAC05, JOBTYP, SEX) |> 
           summary()

                                       JBTP101                       FTPT      
 [-9] Does not apply                       :61818   [-9] Does not apply:32189  
 [-8] No answer                            :    2   [-8] No answer     :   25  
 [1] Working for an employment agency      :  175   [1] Full time      :22538  
 [2] Casual work                           :  302   [2] Part time      : 8314  
 [3] Seasonal work                         :   77   [3] New Deal-FT    :    2  
 [4] Under contract for a fixed period/task:  520   [4] New Deal-PT    :    1  
 [5] Other reason                          :  175                              
                                                             INECAC05    
 [1] Employee                                                    :26365  
 [31] Inactive, not seeking, not like, retired from paid work    :12227  
 [34] Under 16                                                   :11459  
 [2] Self-employed                                               : 4387  
 [27] Inactive, not seeking, not like, long term sick or disabled: 2041  
 [24] Inactive, not seeking, not like, student                   : 1552  
 (Other)                                                         : 5038  
                           JOBTYP              SEX       
 [-9] Does not apply          :36698   [1] Male  :30393  
 [-8] No answer               :   15   [2] Female:32676  
 [1] Permanent                :25104                     
 [2] Not permanent in some way: 1252                     
                                                         
                                                         
                                                         


We can also inspect the description of a variable by looking at its label. Let’s take for example FTPT:

attr(lfs_od24$FTPT,"label")

[1] "Whether working Full or Part Time"


A common way of getting frequency tables in R consists in using table():

t<-table(mydata$FTPT) ### Simple frequency table

t


[-9] Does not apply      [-8] No answer       [1] Full time       [2] Part time 
              32189                  25               22538                8314 
    [3] New Deal-FT     [4] New Deal-PT 
                  2                   1 


We can also examine percentages:

t<- 100*prop.table(t) ### Getting percentage
t


[-9] Does not apply      [-8] No answer       [1] Full time       [2] Part time 
       51.037752303         0.039639125        35.735464333        13.182387544 
    [3] New Deal-FT     [4] New Deal-PT 
        0.003171130         0.001585565 


Finally we can round the percentages in order to make them easier to read:

t<-round(t,1) ### Rounding to one digit

t


[-9] Does not apply      [-8] No answer       [1] Full time       [2] Part time 
               51.0                 0.0                35.7                13.2 
    [3] New Deal-FT     [4] New Deal-PT 
                0.0                 0.0 



QuestionsAnswers



How many cases are there?
What does the variable INECAC05 relate to?
Why are there many missing cases on the variables: JBTP101, FTPT and JOBTYP.




There are 63,069 cases
INECAC05 records NULL
Respondents not in employment are coded as missing values for these variables.




Missing values were recorded as -9 “Does not apply” and -8 “No answer” in the original data.



In order to provide reliable estimates of population values, survey data needs to be weighted when analysed. Weights are variables whose values increase or decrease the relative importance of observations, depending on how likely respondents were to take part to the survey. Some weights are only designed to correct the relative importance of observations, whereas others in addition also enable calculating population totals - the latter are called grossing weights.
Below, we compare weighted and unweighted frequencies and percentages again.
We will be using as_survey_design(), a R function from the survey and srvyr packages that in effect creates a weighted version of our data.
Let us first examine the variable measuring - JOBTYP - whether respondents work in a temporary job or not:

table(mydata$JOBTYP)


          [-9] Does not apply                [-8] No answer 
                        36698                            15 
                [1] Permanent [2] Not permanent in some way 
                        25104                          1252 

round(100*prop.table(table(mydata$JOBTYP)),1)


          [-9] Does not apply                [-8] No answer 
                         58.2                           0.0 
                [1] Permanent [2] Not permanent in some way 
                         39.8                           2.0 


… and create a version without missing values.

mydata <- mydata |> 
                  mutate (
                     JobTmp = ifelse(JOBTYP == "[2] Not permanent in some way",
                                      "Temporary",
                                      "Not temporary"),
                     JobTmp = ifelse(JOBTYP == "[-9] Does not apply" | JOBTYP == "[-8] No answer",
                                      NA,
                                      JobTmp),
                    JobTmp = as.factor(JobTmp)
                  )

table(mydata$JobTmp)


Not temporary     Temporary 
        25104          1252 


Using a function from the survey package, we create a weights-aware version of the data that we will be using for susbsequent analysis:

mydata.s<-mydata|> 
         filter(!is.na(PWT24) ) |> 
         as_survey_design(weights=PWT24)

Please note that we needed to remove observations with missing weights values, in effect observations that should not be taken into account to calculate population values. If we don’t we will get an error message.
We can now compute weighted frequencies and percentages using a survey specific command: svytable():

svytable(~JobTmp, mydata.s)

JobTmp
Not temporary     Temporary 
     27802100       1514206 

round(100*
       prop.table(
         svytable(~JobTmp, mydata.s)
         ),1
      )

JobTmp
Not temporary     Temporary 
         94.8           5.2 





QuestionsAnswers



Do the frequencies change noticeably when the weight is applied?
Create a variable to indicate those working part time and examine weighted and unweighted frequencies.




PWT24 is a grossing weight. Therefore, frequencies now reflect population totals.
The syntax below computes a variable recording whether respondents work part-time or not and produce weighted frequency tables.


 mydata <- mydata |> 
                  mutate (
                    PartTime = ifelse(FTPT == "[4] New Deal-PT" | FTPT  == "[2] Part time",
                                      "Part-time",
                                      "Not part-time"),
                   PartTime = ifelse(FTPT == "[-9] Does not apply" | FTPT == "[-8] No answer",
                                      NA,
                                      PartTime),

                    PartTime = as.factor(PartTime)
                  )


mydata.s<-mydata|> 
         filter(!is.na(PWT24) ) |> 
         as_survey_design(weights=PWT24)

round(100*
       prop.table(
         table(mydata$PartTime)
         ),1
      )


Not part-time     Part-time 
         73.1          26.9 

round(100*
       prop.table(
         svytable(~PartTime, mydata.s)
         ),1
      )

PartTime
Not part-time     Part-time 
         75.2          24.8 









It is straightforward to obtain the percentages of full-time and part-time employees by job tenure, by creating a contingency table:

t1<-svytable(~PartTime+JobTmp,mydata.s)

t1

               JobTmp
PartTime        Not temporary Temporary
  Not part-time      21736784    700619
  Part-time           6060549    812464

            round(
                  100*prop.table(
                   t1
                   ,1) # Requests denominators to be each working time status
                  ,1)

               JobTmp
PartTime        Not temporary Temporary
  Not part-time          96.9       3.1
  Part-time              88.2      11.8


We can add a third variable to the table to simultaneously examine the number of temporary and part-time employees by gender.

t2<-svytable(~PartTime+JobTmp+SEX,mydata.s)

            round(
                  100*prop.table(
                   t2
                   ,3) # Requests denominators to be each gender/working time combination.
                  ,1)

, , SEX = [1] Male

               JobTmp
PartTime        Not temporary Temporary
  Not part-time          85.0       2.7
  Part-time              10.1       2.3

, , SEX = [2] Female

               JobTmp
PartTime        Not temporary Temporary
  Not part-time          63.5       2.1
  Part-time              31.2       3.2





QuestionsAnswers



How many people are temporary employees (all and part-time) in this quarter?
How many females are in part-time temporary employment?
How many applicable cases to we have for the above analysis?




There are 1,514,206 temporary employees.
There are 475,513 females in part-time temporary employment
In order to get the number of valid cases, we need to look at unweighted frequencies. The number of (unweighted) valid cases for this analysis is 26,351




Note: You can check if your results match those in the ONS EMP07 dataset.

title: Weekly earnings of people in employment
text:
In this exercise, you will recreate ONS labour market analysis reported in the table EARN04: Gross weekly earnings of full-time employees [last accessed 21/02/2025]. Currently, this table is updated four times a year in February, May, August and November using data from the Quarterly Labour Force Survey.
Learning outcomes:

To understand better how ONS earnings statistics are produced
To become more familiar with key variables from the QLFS
To learn using income weights appropriately



The data used in this exercise relates to an estimate published by the ONS for October-December 2024.
To follow the exercise, you need to access the relevant dataset from the UK Data Service: Quarterly Labour Force Survey, October - December, 2024.



One you have downloaded the data, save it somewhere accessible, for example in a folder named LFS_exercises. We can now begin analysing the data using R. First let’s load the packages that are are going to need:

library(haven)  ### Functions to open Stata or SPSS datasets
library(dplyr)  ### Easier data manipulation 
library(survey) ### Survey data analysis functions
library(srvyr)  ### Easier  manipulation of survey data

Let’s open the dataset.

## #setwd ("~/LFS_exercises")

lfs_od24 <- read_dta("lfsp_od24_eul_pwt24.dta") ### Importing a Stata format dataset

As there are many variables in the dataset, let’s create a data frame with just the variables we need for the exercise. We can also use this opportunity to convert categorical variables into factors in order to make them easier to understand and manipulate. For greater output clarity, we also remove unused categories of categorical variables using droplevels().

dataex2 <- lfs_od24 |> 
  select(PERSNO, PIWT24, PWT24,GRSSWK, INECAC05, ILODEFR,FTPT, HOURPAY, SEX) |> 
  mutate(
         across(
         c(INECAC05,ILODEFR,FTPT,SEX),\(x) as_factor(x, "both")
               )
         ) |>
  droplevels()




We can use again head() or View() in order to inspect the data and the new variables:

head(dataex2)

# A tibble: 6 × 9
  PERSNO    PIWT24    PWT24     GRSSWK     INECAC05 ILODEFR FTPT  HOURPAY  SEX  
  <dbl+lbl> <dbl+lbl> <dbl+lbl> <dbl+lbl>  <fct>    <fct>   <fct> <dbl+lb> <fct>
1 1         0         706       -9 [Does … [31] In… [3] In… [-9]… -9 [Doe… [2] …
2 2         0         887       -9 [Does … [2] Sel… [1] In… [1] … -9 [Doe… [1] …
3 1         0         598       -9 [Does … [31] In… [3] In… [-9]… -9 [Doe… [2] …
4 1         0         879       -9 [Does … [31] In… [3] In… [-9]… -9 [Doe… [2] …
5 2         0           0       -9 [Does … [31] In… [3] In… [-9]… -9 [Doe… [1] …
6 1         0         793       -9 [Does … [1] Emp… [1] In… [2] … -9 [Doe… [2] …

View(dataex2)




We can also examine descriptive statistics for weekly earnings

summary(dataex2$GRSSWK)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   -9.0    -9.0    -9.0    75.8    -9.0 23076.0 


Non responses are coded using negative values, which may potentially impact on the outcome of statistical analysis. Let’s retain respondents who provided a valid answer only:

summary(dataex2$GRSSWK[dataex2$GRSSWK>0])

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
    5.0   413.2   615.0   732.5   923.0 23076.0 


We could also have a look at weekly earnings using a histogram. Given that income data in general is heavily skewed to the right (a relatively small number respondents with very large earnings), we will restrict the plot to the earnings of 99% of respondents, leaving out the 1% highest earners. These amoung to up to about £2,499 per week.

hist(dataex2$GRSSWK[dataex2$GRSSWK>0 & dataex2$GRSSWK<2500],
     xlab="Earnings (£) -- 1st-99th percentiles",                                           ### x axis label
     main="Gross weekly earnings in the UK, October-December 2024", ### Plot title
     freq=F)                                                        ### Displays probabilities rather than frequencies









QuestionAnswer


Plot the hourly earnings of respondents up to the 99th percentile of earnings



hist(dataex2$HOURPAY[dataex2$HOURPAY>0 & dataex2$HOURPAY<37.5],
     xlab="Earnings (£) -- 1st-99th percentiles",                                                main="Net hourly earnings in the UK, October-December 2024", 
     freq=F)                                                       














It is important to remain mindful of definitions:

Employment refers to people who were both employees and self employed.

title: Weekly earnings of people in employment
text:
The data used in this exercise relates to an estimate published by the ONS for October-December 2024.
To follow the exercise, you need to access the relevant dataset from the UK Data Service: Quarterly Labour Force Survey, October - December, 2024.

title: Weekly earnings of people in employment
text:
One you have downloaded the data, save it somewhere accessible, for example in a folder named LFS_exercises. We can now begin analysing the data using R. First let’s load the packages that are are going to need:

library(haven)  ### Functions to open Stata or SPSS datasets
library(dplyr)  ### Easier data manipulation 
library(survey) ### Survey data analysis functions
library(srvyr)  ### Easier  manipulation of survey data

Let’s open the dataset.

## #setwd ("~/LFS_exercises")

lfs_od24 <- read_dta("lfsp_od24_eul_pwt24.dta") ### Importing a Stata format dataset

As there are many variables in the dataset, let’s create a data frame with just the variables we need for the exercise. We can also use this opportunity to convert categorical variables into factors in order to make them easier to understand and manipulate. For greater output clarity, we also remove unused categories of categorical variables using droplevels().

dataex2 <- lfs_od24 |> 
  select(PERSNO, PIWT24, PWT24,GRSSWK, INECAC05, ILODEFR,FTPT, HOURPAY, SEX) |> 
  mutate(
         across(
         c(INECAC05,ILODEFR,FTPT,SEX),\(x) as_factor(x, "both")
               )
         ) |>
  droplevels()

title: Working with the Labour Force Survey
text:
A first exercise designed to help people get familar with the QLFS - size, key variables, the main weight, the effect of the grossing weight on counts.



A follow up exercise using the QLFS but focusing on earnings - key earnings variables, the earnings weight and when not to use the earnings weight.



Using the Labour Force Survey Two-Quarter Longitudinal Dataset - introduces the longitudinal datasets - the structure of the dataset, key variables for examining flows, longitudinal weights



Producing an estimate with CI using different weighting approaches, adjusting the CI using published design factors.
